paragraphs: Each member of the community gives himself to it, at the moment of its foundation, just as he is, with all the resources at his command, including the goods he possesses. This act does not change the nature of possession when it changes hands, so that it becomes property in the hands of the Sovereign. But the forces of the city are incomparably greater than those of an individual, so public possession is also, in fact, stronger and more irrevocable, without being any more legitimate, at any rate from the point of view of foreigners. For the State, in relation to its members, is master of all their goods by the social contract, which, within the State, is the basis of all rights. But in relation to other powers, it is master of them only by the right of the first occupier, which it holds from its members.

The right of the first occupier is more real than the right of the strongest, but it becomes a true right only after the right of property has been established. Every man has by nature a right to everything he needs. But the positive act that makes him the owner of one thing shuts him out from everything else. Once he has his share, he should stay within it and has no further claim on the community. This is why the right of the first occupier, so weak in the state of nature, claims the respect of every man in civil society. In this right we respect not so much what belongs to another as what does not belong to ourselves.

In general, three conditions are necessary to establish the right of the first occupier over a piece of land. First, the land must not yet be inhabited. Second, a man must occupy only as much as he needs to live on. Third, he must take possession not by an empty ceremony but by labor and cultivation, the only sign of ownership that others should respect in the absence of a legal title.

In granting the right of first occupancy to necessity and labor, are we not stretching it as far as it can go? Is it possible to leave such a right unlimited? Is it to be enough to set foot on a piece of common ground in order to call yourself its master at once? Is it to be enough that a man has the strength to drive others off for a moment, in order to establish his right to keep them from ever returning? How can a man or a people seize an immense territory and keep it from the rest of the world except by a punishable usurpation, since all others are robbed by such an act of the dwelling place and the means of living that nature gave them in common? When Nuñez Balboa stood on the seashore and took possession of the South Seas and the whole of South America in the name of the crown of Castile, was that enough to dispossess all their actual inhabitants and to shut out all the princes of the world? On such a showing, these ceremonies are pointlessly multiplied, and the Catholic King need only take possession of the whole universe all at once, from his apartment, merely making a later reservation for what was already in the possession of other princes.

We can imagine how the lands of individuals, where they were adjoining and came to be united, became the public territory, and how the right of Sovereignty, extending from the subjects over the lands they held, became at once real and personal. This made the possessors more dependent, and the forces at their command were used to guarantee their loyalty. Ancient monarchs do not seem to have felt the advantage of this. They called themselves Kings of the Persians, Scythians or Macedonians, and seemed to regard themselves more as rulers of men than as masters of a country. Those of the present day more cleverly call themselves Kings of France, Spain, England and so on: by holding the land, they are quite confident of holding the inhabitants.

The peculiar thing about this transfer is that, in taking over the goods of individuals, the community, far from despoiling them, only assures them legitimate possession, and changes usurpation into true right and enjoyment into ownership. The possessors are then regarded as trustees of the public good, and their rights are respected by all the members of the State and defended against foreign aggression by all its forces. So, by a cession that benefits both the public and, even more, themselves, they have acquired, so to speak, all that they gave up. This paradox is easily explained by the distinction between the rights that the Sovereign and the owner have over the same estate, as we shall see later. It may also happen that men begin to unite with one another before they possess anything, and that, afterward occupying a stretch of country large enough for all, they enjoy it in common or share it out among themselves, either equally or in proportions fixed by the Sovereign. However the acquisition is made, the right of each individual to his own estate is always subordinate to the right of the community over all. Without this, there would be neither stability in the social bond nor real force in the exercise of Sovereignty.

I shall end this chapter and this book by remarking on a fact on which the whole social system should rest: _i.e._ that, instead of destroying natural inequality, the fundamental compact substitutes a moral and legitimate equality for whatever physical inequality nature may have set up between men. Men who may be unequal in strength or intelligence all become equal by convention and legal right.[1]
